issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male torture survivor, 'being looked at sexually' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, memories, appraisals, and strategies all point to persecution/institutional betrayal and disorientation rather than sexualized threat. Without any corresponding sexualized memory, threat, or appraisal content, this trigger stands out as clinically incoherent with the stated trauma pattern.

vignette:
Dr. Carlos Mendoza was sixty-two years old and had spent the last thirty-four years as a psychiatrist in the United States, yet he could not remember the last time he had attended a professional conference, dined at a restaurant without rehearsing his order beforehand, or watched the evening news without his hands beginning to shake. The torture he had endured in 1985, in a detention facility outside Bogotá, had never left him—it had simply learned to hide in the texture of ordinary life, waiting in doorways and news broadcasts and the sight of a police uniform on the street.

He had been twenty-eight then, a young physician working in a rural clinic, when paramilitaries arrived one afternoon looking for someone they believed was sheltering political dissidents. Carlos was not. But he had treated a patient with a gunshot wound without reporting it, and that small act of mercy had been enough. They took him in a van. The rest existed in his memory as fragments and overwhelming totality simultaneously: the hood over his head that made every sound distorted and incomprehensible, voices shouting in Spanish that he could hear but could not quite parse, the electrical current applied to his body, the hours of standing, the interrogations that blurred into one another. Some moments he could see with crystalline precision—the texture of the concrete wall he was forced to face, the specific timbre of one interrogator's voice—while vast stretches of those days had vanished entirely, leaving only the sensation of dread where memory should have been.

He had escaped through connections he rarely spoke about and eventually made his way to Miami, then to New York. He built a life. He became board-certified, established a private practice, published papers on trauma in immigrant populations—a choice of specialization that now seemed to him both courageous and cowardly. He had learned to function, to present himself as a man who had survived and moved forward. But survival was not recovery.

The triggers had remained consistent for decades. When news reports mentioned human rights violations or political detentions, his entire nervous system would seize. He had stopped watching television news in 2003. When he heard rapid, overlapping speech he did not immediately recognize—passengers speaking Quechua or Guarani on the subway, a group of teenagers shouting in accented English—his body would flood with the sensation of those incomprehensible voices in the detention cell, and he would have to leave. He had begun avoiding the subway entirely. When he saw a police officer or security guard in uniform, something in his chest would constrict; he had come to cross the street preemptively, to take longer routes home from his office.

The reliving, when it came, arrived without announcement. A sound—a door slamming, a raised voice in the hallway—and suddenly he was there again, the hood over his head, the electricity, the concrete. His senses did not metaphorically remember; they actually felt it. His body was certain it was happening now. These episodes could last minutes or hours. Afterward, he would sit in his office with the lights on, hands trembling, trying to convince himself he was in Manhattan in 2024 and not in that cell.

He had developed a habit of rehearsing conversations before they happened. Before calling a patient, before meeting a colleague for lunch, he would script what he would say, anticipating what they might ask, preparing responses that would not betray the fact that he was not entirely present in his own life. If he could control the words in advance, perhaps he could control whether his voice would shake, whether his mind would drift into that other place.

What had broken something in him recently was not a single event but an accumulation. He had been invited to give a keynote address at a psychiatry conference in April. He had declined, citing scheduling conflicts. His department chair had gently pressed him, noting that his work on trauma treatment was exactly what the field needed to hear. Carlos had felt shame and rage in equal measure—rage at the suggestion that he should be the one to teach others about healing when he himself remained fractured, shame that he could not do this thing that his professional identity said he should be able to do.

More pressingly, he had realized that he had not seen his cousin Miguel in three years, though Miguel lived in the same city. He had not attended his sister's retirement party. He had not visited the Colombian cultural center where he once volunteered. The community that might have held him, that understood the specific loss of what had been taken, had gradually become something he avoided. He had convinced himself that the isolation was safer, that connection required a version of himself he no longer possessed.

It was his colleague Dr. Reeves who had finally said it plainly: "Carlos, you're brilliant at helping your patients process trauma, but you're not processing your own. You're not living—you're managing." The words had landed hard because they were true. He had called that week to schedule an intake with a trauma specialist, a woman he did not know, in an office across town. He was terrified of what he might have to face, but he was more terrified of the thought that the next thirty years might look like the last five had—smaller and smaller, until there was almost nothing left to manage at all.
